subject: history
title: 1937–1945: when the world war started in China
dek: Marco Polo Bridge to surrender — a war already eight years old when many textbooks open in Poland.
text: 1937–1945: when the world war started in China Marco Polo Bridge to surrender — a war already eight years old when many textbooks open in Poland. 1937–1945 (with 1931 behind it) This capsule is the Second World War from China, not a European war with an Asian chapter. Death-toll figures for Nanjing remain contested; the text says so instead of picking a round number for effect. One photograph of a bombed street is enough. There are no pictures of bodies used as decoration. History history 1931 Mukden 18 September: a railway explosion, then the Kwantung Army occupies Manchuria. 1932 Manchukuo A puppet state. The Lytton Commission reports; the League does not stop it. 1937 7 July Marco Polo Bridge. Full-scale war. Shanghai in August; Nanjing in December. 1937–38 Nanjing City falls 13 December 1937. Killings, rape, and looting into January 1938. 1939 Europe Germany invades Poland, 1 September. Many English textbooks still start the world war here. 1941 The wars join Pearl Harbor, 7 December. The China war and the European war become one Allied war. The date the textbook still uses A great many English-language textbooks still open the Second World War on 1 September 1939, when Germany invaded Poland. China had been in full-scale war since 7 July 1937, and under occupation in the Northeast since 1931. The 1939 date is not a lie about Europe. It is a habit of where the narrator is standing. Mukden Incident 18 September 九一八 On the night of 18 September 1931 a section of the South Manchuria Railway near Mukden (Shenyang) was blown up. The Kwantung Army blamed Chinese saboteurs and used the explosion to occupy Manchuria. Later evidence treats the blast as a Japanese pretext. Manchukuo Manchoukuo Puppet state proclaimed in 1932 in occupied Northeast China, with Puyi as chief executive and later emperor. Few governments recognized it. It lasted until 1945. Lytton Report Lytton Commission League of Nations commission (Lord Lytton) that investigated Manchuria and reported in 1932: Japan’s action was not self-defense; Manchukuo was not a genuine independence movement. The League adopted the report; it did not reverse the occupation. Japan left the League in 1933. Nanjing decade 1927–1937: the Nationalist government, having nominally unified China, made Nanjing its capital. “Decade” is a historian’s label for a state-building interval that ended when the capital had to be abandoned. Marco Polo Bridge 盧溝橋 Lugou Bridge Stone bridge southwest of Beijing. On 7 July 1937 a Japanese night exercise, a missing soldier, and shots at Wanping became the start of full-scale war. The missing soldier turned up; the war did not stop. United Front Second United Front The uneasy KMT–CCP alliance against Japan after the Xi’an Incident (December 1936) and the 1937 invasion. It was a wartime necessity, not a reconciliation. It frayed long before 1945. comfort women 慰安婦 The Japanese military’s system of sexual slavery in occupied Asia — stations staffed by women from Korea, China, the Philippines, and elsewhere, under coercion and deception. A regional system, not a single camp. The documentary record and survivor testimony are the sources; this capsule does not illustrate it with a photograph. Chongqing Chungking 重慶 The Nationalist wartime capital after Nanjing and Wuhan. From 1938 to 1943 it was repeatedly bombed by Japanese aircraft — one of the war’s long air campaigns against a civilian city. Nanjing massacre Nanking Massacre Rape of Nanking After Japanese forces took Nanjing on 13 December 1937, weeks of killing, rape, and looting followed into January 1938. Death-toll estimates remain contested: the International Military Tribunal for the Far East cited over 200,000; the official PRC figure is 300,000. The event is not in doubt because the totals differ. Kwantung Army Japanese army in the leased Kwantung Territory and, after 1931, in Manchuria. It often acted ahead of civilian government in Tokyo. Mukden is the usual example. Xi’an Incident December 1936: Zhang Xueliang detained Chiang Kai-shek in Xi’an and forced a turn toward resisting Japan rather than only encircling the Communists. The Second United Front follows. Burma Road Overland supply route from Burma into Yunnan, used after Japan closed the China coast. When Burma fell in 1942 the airlift over “the Hump” replaced it. Allied films made the road a miracle; it was also a desperate substitute for ports. memory politics How a state teaches a war afterward: which dates, which victims, which silences. PRC, Taiwan, and Japan do not tell 1937–45 the same way. The disagreement is part of the after, not a reason to treat the war as undecidable. Before A railway charge, a puppet state, a capital that still believed in time On the night of 18 September 1931 a section of the South Manchuria Railway near Mukden was blown up. The Kwantung Army blamed Chinese saboteurs and occupied the Northeast. Later evidence treats the blast as a Japanese pretext. The League of Nations sent the Lytton Commission. The 1932 report said Japan had not acted in self-defense and that Manchukuo was not a real independence movement. The League adopted the report. It did not put the army back. Japan left the League in 1933. The Lytton Commission at a railway site in Manchuria. A photograph of inspection, not of enforcement. The report of 1932 is clearer than the League’s power to act on it. Members of the Lytton Commission inspecting a railway site in Manchuria. In those same years the Nationalist government was trying to be a state from Nanjing — the “Nanjing decade,” 1927–1937: ministries, a currency, campaigns against the Communists, a capital that still looked like a future. The decade is a historian’s interval. It ends when the capital has to move. The era A night at a bridge, then a country on the road On 7 July 1937 Japanese troops on night exercise near the Marco Polo Bridge (盧溝橋), southwest of Beijing, reported a missing soldier and shots at Wanping. The soldier turned up. The firing did not become a local incident. Within weeks it was a war. Shanghai was fought over from August to November. The government left Nanjing. Shanghai, 1937: a cart, furniture, one man. U.S. Navy photograph. The unnamed person in this war is usually on the road — out of Hongkou, out of Nanjing, west toward Wuhan and then Chongqing. Armies have names in the captions. Refugees often do not. A man pulling a heavily loaded refugee cart through a Shanghai street in 1937. Japanese forces entered Nanjing on 13 December 1937. For weeks into January 1938 there were mass killings, rape, and looting. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East later cited a death toll of over 200,000; the official figure of the People’s Republic is 300,000. Historians still argue about the arithmetic. They do not argue about whether the weeks happened. This capsule uses one photograph of a street already bombed in September — not a picture of corpses. Pingshi Street, Nanjing, after the raid of 28 September 1937 — months before the December occupation. A ruined commercial street, not a massacre photograph. It is here to show that the city was already being broken from the air before the army arrived. A ruined shopping street in Nanjing after a Japanese air raid on 28 September 1937. The capital that remained was Chongqing: fog, stairs, and, from 1938 into 1943, repeated Japanese bombing. It was one of the long air campaigns of the war against a civilian city. People dug shelters into the rock. The government that sat there was still Chiang’s. A Mitsubishi Ki-21 over Chongqing. The picture is from the bomber’s side of the air. What it does not show is the city underneath — the shelters, the fires, the years of it. A Japanese Mitsubishi Ki-21 bomber over Chongqing during an air raid. The Second United Front put the Nationalists and the Communists in the same war against Japan. It was a cease-fire with a shared enemy, not a merger. Zhou Enlai spent much of the war as the Communist representative in the Nationalist capitals. The front frayed. It did not wait for 1945 to fail. Across occupied Asia the Japanese military ran a system of sexual slavery later named 慰安婦 / comfort women: stations, contracts that were not contracts, women from Korea, China, the Philippines, and elsewhere. It was a regional system, not a single atrocity attached to one city. The sources are documents and survivors. This capsule does not put a face on it for layout. Look outward from China, not the other way around. On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland. That is a real beginning — of the European war. It is not the beginning of this one. For two years the China war and the European war run in parallel. They join after 7 December 1941, when Japan attacks Pearl Harbor and the Western colonies in Southeast Asia, and the United States declares war. 1941 is the year the wars become one Allied war. It is not the year China entered. People A generalissimo, a liaison, a writer, and the unnamed Chiang Kai-shek 蔣介石 1887–1975 Head of the Nationalist state and of the army that had to trade space for time. This capsule does not need him to be a hero or a villain. It needs him as the man whose government moved west and whose army did not defeat Japan alone. Chiang in Shanghai, 1937 — a front-line photograph meant to raise morale. It is a posed closeness to the army, not a biography. Zhou Enlai 周恩來 1898–1976 Communist representative in the Nationalist wartime capitals. The United Front’s human hinge. After 1949 he is someone else. Here he is the man in the shared city. Wuhan, summer 1938: Zhou Enlai and Deng Yingchao with the American journalist Edgar Snow. A United Front photograph — Communist liaison, Nationalist wartime capital, foreign press. Xiao Hong 蕭紅 1911–1942 Writer, from the Northeast. The Field of Life and Death; Tales of Hulan River. She fled Harbin, wrote in the same years the armies moved, and died in Hong Kong in 1942. Not a general. A person the war displaced and then outlived. Xiao Hong. The file is a small period portrait; it is what a free archive has. She died in Japanese-occupied Hong Kong in 1942. The unnamed on the road 1937–1945 Millions moved west. The photographs usually say “refugees.” The word is accurate and too small. They are the reason a capital in Chongqing still had a country attached to it. Shanghai, 1937. One cart, no name on the Navy caption. After Surrender, then another war, then the argument about memory Japan surrendered in August 1945. In China the United Front was already a fiction. Full-scale civil war between Nationalists and Communists ran from 1946 to 1949. The People’s Republic was proclaimed in Beijing; the Nationalist government moved to Taiwan. The war against Japan became a founding story for more than one state. Memory politics is the after that does not end. The PRC, Taiwan, and Japan do not teach 1937–45 as the same syllabus: different dates of emphasis, different silences, different uses of Nanjing and of 慰安婦. Disagreement about the telling is not the same as disagreement about whether the war occurred. Europe’s 1939 remains the other theater — a real war, started later, that textbooks still use as the world’s first page. A question Leave this on the table If your textbook begins the world war in 1939, whose war has it decided not to open with? Why We Fight: The Battle of China (U.S. Army, 1944) Frank Capra’s public-domain U.S. Army film. It is wartime Allied propaganda — useful as a primary source for how Washington explained China in 1944, not as a neutral history. Internet Archive. National Archives copy of the same film NARA identifier 36072 / 111-OF-6. Same picture, institutional catalogue. Still a 1944 briefing film, including atrocity footage the Army wanted soldiers to see.

subject: literature
title: High Modernism (c. 1910–1930): the sentence breaks
dek: Woolf, Joyce, Eliot — and, in the same years, 新青年 and Lu Xun’s broken “I.”
text: High Modernism (c. 1910–1930): the sentence breaks Woolf, Joyce, Eliot — and, in the same years, 新青年 and Lu Xun’s broken “I.” c. 1910–1930 “High modernism” is a later classroom name for a cluster of difficult, self-conscious works written mostly in English, French, and German around the 1910s–1920s. It was never a membership. This capsule uses the name, then looks at the same decades in Chinese vernacular writing — not as an appendix, as the same years. Literature literature 1914–18 The war European high modernism is unintelligible if you subtract the First World War. 1915 新青年 Chen Duxiu founds Youth Magazine in Shanghai; it is renamed 新青年 the next year. 1918 Two broken “I”s Lu Xun’s 狂人日記 in 新青年; Ulysses begins to appear in The Little Review. 1922 The year of the pile Ulysses (book), The Waste Land, Jacob’s Room. A convenient classroom date, and a real cluster. 1925–27 Woolf Mrs Dalloway; To the Lighthouse. Stream of consciousness as a method, not a mood. 1921–22 阿Q Lu Xun’s 阿Q正傳 serialized. The vernacular “I” and the village as national allegory. 1918, twice In May 1918 Lu Xun’s 狂人日記 appeared in 新青年. That same year The Little Review in New York began serializing Joyce’s Ulysses. Two broken first persons, two little magazines, no transatlantic plot connecting them. The coincidence is chronological, which is enough. stream of consciousness A way of writing that follows a mind’s associations rather than a plot summary. The phrase is older than Woolf; the method, in English, is often attached to her and to Joyce. It is a technique, not a personality type. little magazines little magazine Low-circulation journals that printed work commercial houses would not: The Little Review, The Egoist, Blast, 新青年. Modernism’s distribution system was often a cheap periodical, not a first edition. Blast Vorticist magazine, two issues, 1914 and 1915, edited by Wyndham Lewis. The pink cover is easier to remember than the poems. It is one of the little magazines, not the movement’s bible. The Waste Land T. S. Eliot’s 1922 poem, first in The Criterion and The Dial, then as a book with notes. Fragment, quotation, and a London that sounds like a ruin. Eliot later converted; the poem is not a sermon. Ulysses James Joyce’s novel of one Dublin day (16 June 1904), serialized from 1918, published as a book in Paris in 1922. The Little Review’s editors were convicted of obscenity in the U.S. in 1921 for printing it. May Fourth 五四 May Fourth Movement 4 May 1919: Beijing student protests against the Versailles settlement and Chinese diplomats. In literary history the name also covers the wider New Culture years — vernacular writing, 新青年, a fight with classical prose. 新青年 New Youth La Jeunesse 青年杂志 Magazine founded by Chen Duxiu in Shanghai in 1915 as 青年杂志, renamed 新青年 in 1916. Democracy, science, vernacular literature. Lu Xun’s 狂人日記 appeared there in May 1918. 狂人日記 A Madman’s Diary Diary of a Madman Lu Xun’s 1918 story: a first-person diary that reads Confucian virtue as cannibalism. Classical Chinese in the preface, vernacular in the diary. The broken “I” is the point. 阿Q正傳 The True Story of Ah Q Lu Xun’s 1921–22 serial. Ah Q, a village nobody who wins by telling himself he has won. Read as national allegory, as class comedy, and as a study of humiliation. vernacular 白話 baihua Writing in the spoken language rather than classical Chinese (文言). May Fourth writers treated 白話 as a political choice: who gets to read, and who the nation is imagined to be. free indirect free indirect style A third-person sentence that takes on a character’s diction without quotation marks. Woolf uses it constantly. It is one reason her “he” and “she” do not behave like a stable Victorian narrator. Harlem Renaissance African American literary and arts flowering in the 1920s, centered in Harlem. Contemporaneous with high modernism, not a footnote to it. Different magazines, different constraints, same decade. Mrs Dalloway Woolf’s 1925 novel: one June day in London, a party, a shell-shocked man. The war is inside the sentences, not only in the plot. Before The stable narrator Nineteenth-century realist and naturalist novels — in English, French, Russian — often trusted a narrator who could stand outside the scene and tell you what it meant. Even when the news was grim, the grammar was stable. Someone was in charge of the sentence. That stability was already under pressure before 1914: interior monologue in Dostoevsky, Flaubert’s free indirect style, late James. High modernism does not invent inwardness. It breaks the sentence that used to carry it, and it does so after a war that made the old voice sound like a lie. The era Fragments, magazines, and more than one vernacular The First World War is not background music. Eliot’s The Waste Land (1922) is a poem that cannot keep a single voice; quotation and ruin do the work a narrator used to do. Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway (1925) puts a shell-shocked man and a party on the same June day. Joyce’s Ulysses (serialized from 1918, book 1922) gives one Dublin day more interior traffic than a nineteenth-century decade. Blast no. 1, 1914 — Wyndham Lewis’s Vorticist magazine, two issues and a war. Little magazines were modernism’s cheap distribution system. The cover is easier to remember than most of the poems inside. Pink-and-black cover of the first issue of Blast magazine, 1914, with the title in huge diagonal letters. James Joyce in Zurich, about 1918 — the year Ulysses began to appear in The Little Review. The photograph was later used on a 1921 subscription form for the book, which is why it is public domain in the United States. James Joyce in Zurich, photograph by Camille Ruf, about 1918. Stream of consciousness is a method: follow the mind’s jump, do not tidy it for the drawing room. Free indirect style lets a third-person sentence wear a character’s clothes. Fragmentation after 1918 is not only a trick. It is a claim that the old continuous voice had been a luxury. T. S. Eliot in 1920, from a snapshot by Lady Ottoline Morrell (d. 1938). Two years later The Waste Land. The snapshot is small and informal on purpose: this is not the later, public Eliot of the readings. Snapshot of T. S. Eliot in 1920, cropped from a photograph by Lady Ottoline Morrell. The same years, in Chinese. Chen Duxiu’s 新青年 (first 青年杂志, 1915) argued for vernacular 白話 against classical 文言 — who gets to read, and what a national literature is allowed to sound like. On 4 May 1919 students in Beijing protested the Versailles settlement; “May Fourth” later names both that day and the wider New Culture years. Lu Xun’s 狂人日記 (May 1918) puts a diary in the vernacular and a preface in classical, then lets the diary say that virtue is eating people. 阿Q正傳 (1921–22) makes a village nobody into a national problem. The broken “I” is not a London export. It is a contemporaneous solution to a different classical inheritance. A surviving copy of 新青年 / La Jeunesse, photographed in a museum case. The French subtitle is on the cover for a reason: the magazine argued in Chinese and looked, deliberately, toward Europe. Lu Xun’s 狂人日記 appeared in its pages in 1918. A bound copy of 新青年 (La Jeunesse) displayed in a museum case, French title visible on the cover. Lu Xun, 1930 — after the stories this capsule is about, still the face later textbooks freeze. He died in 1936. Early photographs of him are in the public domain in China and, as tagged here, in the United States. Studio portrait of Lu Xun, 1930. Also in the same decade, not in the same magazines: the Harlem Renaissance in the United States. Different constraints, different editors, a modernism that had to argue for the right to be modern. High modernism as an English-department brand is too small for 1922 if it can only hold Eliot. People Three English names, one Chinese one Virginia Woolf 1882–1941 Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927), A Room of One’s Own (1929). The sentences move as a mind moves. The war is in the jumps, not only in the plot. Beresford portrait, 1902. James Joyce 1882–1941 Dubliners, A Portrait, then Ulysses. Exile, serialization, a ban, a Paris book. The method is excess: more interior than a day should hold. Zurich, about 1918. T. S. Eliot 1888–1965 American-born, London-settled. The Waste Land (1922) as the syllabus poem of fragmentation. Later he becomes a public Christian conservative. The poem and the later man are not required to agree. Snapshot, 1920. Lu Xun 魯迅 1881–1936 狂人日記 (1918), 阿Q正傳 (1921–22). Vernacular as a weapon against a classical prose that had pretended to be virtue. Same decades as Woolf and Joyce; a different broken “I.” 1930 studio portrait. After Reaction, then other modernisms By the 1930s and 1940s a reaction is already audible: calls for plainer prose, political clarity, a novel that will do something. Mid-century English and American fiction often treats high modernism as a brilliant dead end. That verdict is a period style of its own. Later postcolonial writers — in English and out of it — take the broken sentence and the unreliable “I” into other empires. They are not a delayed May Fourth or a delayed Woolf. They are what happens when the method leaves the original capitals. A question Leave this on the table If the narrator is no longer stable, who is the “we” in “we moderns”? 狂人日記 — Chinese text on Wikisource The 1918 story is in the public domain. This is the text, not a dramatization. Ulysses — full 1922 text at Project Gutenberg Joyce’s novel is public domain in the United States. Gutenberg’s HTML/plain text, not a spoken abridgment. Mrs Dalloway — Project Gutenberg Woolf’s 1925 novel (Gutenberg #71865), public domain in the U.S. The book, not a film, and not the earlier short story “Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street.”

subject: film
title: French New Wave (c. 1958–1964): the cut that showed the cut
dek: Critics pick up cameras in Paris; jump cuts, streets, and the idea that a film has an author.
text: French New Wave (c. 1958–1964): the cut that showed the cut Critics pick up cameras in Paris; jump cuts, streets, and the idea that a film has an author. c. 1958–1964 “Nouvelle Vague” was a press label, then a useful pile of films. It was never one manifesto. Cahiers critics (Truffaut, Godard, Chabrol, Rohmer, Rivette) are one cluster. The so-called Left Bank (Varda, Resnais, Marker) is another. This capsule stays with 1958–1964 and does not pirate the features. Film film 1954 A certain tendency Truffaut’s Cahiers essay attacks the “cinéma de qualité” and argues for the director as author. 1955 Varda first Agnès Varda’s La Pointe Courte — often treated as a New Wave film before the name exists. 1959 Cannes Les 400 coups. Truffaut, late of Cahiers, wins Best Director. 1960 Breathless À bout de souffle. Jump cuts, handheld, Paris streets, a plot that refuses to behave. 1959–64 Same years, elsewhere Oshima and Imamura in Japan; Free Cinema’s afterlife in Britain; Italy after neorealism. 1967– The after New Hollywood learns that a film can announce its making. Taiwan New Cinema is a later cousin. Varda was already there Agnès Varda’s La Pointe Courte was released in 1955 — four years before Les 400 coups, and before “Nouvelle Vague” was a headline. She was a photographer, not a Cahiers critic. If the story of the New Wave begins only when the boys from the magazine pick up cameras, the date is wrong. cinéma de qualité tradition de qualité The postwar French studio manner that Cahiers writers attacked: literary adaptations, polished craftsmen, little visible author. Truffaut’s 1954 essay “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français” is the famous insult. Cahiers du cinéma Cahiers Paris film magazine, founded 1951. In the 1950s it is where Truffaut, Godard, Rivette, Rohmer, and Chabrol learned to argue. Several of them then made the films they had been asking for. auteur politique des auteurs The Cahiers claim that a director can be the author of a film the way a novelist is the author of a book — visible across a body of work, even inside a studio system. It is a critical method, later flattened into a compliment. jump cut jump cuts An edit that leaves a visible gap in time inside a continuous shot. Breathless made the device famous. It is not a mistake that slipped through; it is the film showing you the cut. caméra-stylo Alexandre Astruc’s 1948 phrase: the camera as a pen. New Wave directors used it to mean that a film could be as personal, and as written, as a novel. It is a metaphor, not a camera model. location shooting Shooting in real streets and apartments instead of only on a soundstage. Cheaper, faster, and part of the look: Paris as itself, available light, passers-by who did not sign a release in advance. montage In ordinary French, “editing.” In film theory it also names a tradition (Soviet montage) that builds meaning by collision between shots, as opposed to the long take that lets a scene play. New Wave films use both, and sometimes refuse the choice. Left Bank Later nickname for Varda, Resnais, Marker and others — less Cahiers-cinephile, more literary and documentary. Useful as a cluster, not a membership card. Varda’s La Pointe Courte (1955) predates the 1959 boom. Free Cinema British documentary movement of the mid-1950s (Anderson, Reisz, Richardson) that also treated everyday life as worth filming. Not a French franchise; a contemporaneous argument about who gets to be on screen. Japanese New Wave Nuberu Bagu Studio and independent Japanese films of the late 1950s–60s (Ōshima, Imamura, Yoshida, and others) that broke with studio polish in the same years as the Nouvelle Vague. The Japanese name ヌーベルバーグ is a loan; the films are not a sequel. Les 400 coups The 400 Blows 400 Blows François Truffaut’s first feature, 1959. Antoine Doinel (Jean-Pierre Léaud) as a boy the school and the home cannot hold. The English title is a mistranslation of a French idiom about raising hell. À bout de souffle Breathless Jean-Luc Godard’s first feature, 1960, from a story Truffaut sold him. Michel and Patricia, a stolen car, a killing, Paris. The jump cuts are the part everyone remembers; the film is also about movie-love as a way of walking. Raoul Coutard Cinematographer on Breathless, Jules et Jim, and other New Wave features. Handheld, available light, fast film stock. The look people mean when they say “it was shot in the street.” Before Quality, and a magazine that hated it Postwar French popular cinema had a manner the Cahiers du cinéma writers learned to insult: cinéma de qualité. Literary properties, careful craftsmen, stars in period dress, a film that did not look as if anyone in particular had wanted it. The insult is unfair to some of those craftsmen. It was also a way of clearing a desk. In 1954 François Truffaut published “Une certaine tendance du cinéma français.” The essay argues that the director, not the screenwriter-adapter, should be the author — the politique des auteurs. Alexandre Astruc had already called the camera a pen (caméra-stylo) in 1948. Theory here is not a seminar add-on. It is a set of fighting words that several of the fighters then had to live up to. An Éclair Caméflex — a French camera light enough to leave the studio. New Wave legend leans on handheld cameras and fast film. The Caméflex is one of the actual objects in that legend. (Cahiers covers from the 1950s are still in copyright; this machine is not a still from Breathless.) Rear view of an Éclair Caméflex motion-picture camera, the lightweight French camera associated with New Wave location shooting. They were not the first people to be tired of polish. Italian neorealism had already taken cameras into streets and hired non-actors. In Britain, Free Cinema shorts (mid-1950s) treated factory gates and dance halls as worth filming. Paris in 1958 is one capital in a wider argument about what a film is allowed to look like. The era Streets, cuts, and who counts as an author 1959 is the year the press needed a name. Les 400 coups premiered at Cannes; Truffaut, who had been banned from the festival as a critic, won Best Director as a filmmaker. Alain Resnais’s Hiroshima mon amour and Claude Chabrol’s Les Cousins belong to the same season. The “wave” is a cluster of first features, not a studio program. À bout de souffle followed in 1960. Godard shot Paris with Raoul Coutard, often handheld, often in available light, and then cut in a way that left the joins visible. A jump cut is not a stumble. It is the film admitting it is made of pieces. That is what “the cut that showed the cut” means here: montage as something you are allowed to notice, not only as invisible grammar. An Arriflex 16 — another lightweight camera of the period. 16mm and portable 35mm let people shoot without booking a studio for a month. The New Wave look is partly an aesthetic and partly a budget. An Arriflex 16mm motion-picture camera on a wooden surface. Agnès Varda is not an extra in this story. La Pointe Courte (1955) is already a New Wave film by later definition: location, non-professionals, a director who had not come up through the industry ladder. Cléo de 5 à 7 (1962) walks a woman through real Paris time. If “auteur” only fits the Cahiers men, the word is doing advertising, not criticism. Agnès Varda (left) with Corinne Marchand at Venice, 1962, the year of Cléo de 5 à 7. A festival portrait, not a film still. Varda is in the same years as Truffaut and Godard, not in a later chapter labeled “also women.” Agnès Varda standing beside Corinne Marchand at the Venice Film Festival in 1962. What “theory” means on these sets is practical. Auteur: someone is responsible for the film as a whole, including its faults. Montage versus scene: do you build meaning by colliding shots, or by letting a block of time play? The New Wave did not pick one church. It made the choice visible. A film could announce that it was being made — look at the camera, break the match cut, quote another movie out loud. The same years, elsewhere. In Japan, Ōshima Nagisa’s Cruel Story of Youth (1960) and Imamura Shōhei’s early features break with studio polish while Godard is cutting Breathless — not as a later “influence,” as a contemporaneous fight inside a different studio system. In Britain, the Free Cinema names move into features (Saturday Night and Sunday Morning, 1960). In Italy, the generation after neorealism (Antonioni, Fellini already famous; Pasolini’s Accattone is 1961) is also arguing about modern life on screen. Paris is one city in that argument. People Critics, a photographer, a camera operator François Truffaut 1932–1984 Cahiers critic, then director. Les 400 coups (1959) makes Antoine Doinel and makes Truffaut suddenly respectable. The man who had insulted the industry now had to shoot on time and cut a film an audience would sit through. Jean-Luc Godard 1930–2022 The other Cahiers name everyone uses as shorthand. Breathless is the calling card; the later 1960s are a different, more militant argument. This capsule stops before Week-end. Agnès Varda 1928–2019 Photographer first. La Pointe Courte (1955), Cléo de 5 à 7 (1962). Not a guest in the boys’ magazine. A director whose dates sit inside the wave, not after it. Venice, 1962. Ōshima Nagisa 1932–2013 Japanese studio rebel, then independent. Cruel Story of Youth (1960) is the same year as Breathless. He is here as a contemporary, not as proof that Paris invented youth cinema and Tokyo borrowed it. After New Hollywood, and a delayed cousin American studio films of the late 1960s and 1970s — the pile later called New Hollywood — learned that a film could look handmade: location, jumpier editing, a director whose name was part of the sale. Bonnie and Clyde (1967) is the usual bridge example; the traffic of influence is real and also over-told. Taiwan New Cinema in the 1980s (Hou Hsiao-hsien, Edward Yang, and others) is sometimes filed under “New Wave” in English. It is a delayed cousin, not a contemporaneous peer: different decade, different political problem, a long take more often than a jump cut. It belongs in After, not in 1960. The lasting idea is simpler than the brand. A film can announce its making. Once audiences have seen the cut, they cannot be told that films just happen. A question Leave this on the table If you can see the cut, who do you think is responsible for the film? Annette Insdorf — “The 400 Blows: Close to Home” (Criterion) A legal essay on the Criterion site, not the feature. Use it as a way into the film; do not expect a free stream of Les 400 coups here. BFI — “10 great French New Wave films” A curator’s list from the British Film Institute. It is a guide to legal viewing, not a pirate archive. BFI — “Where to begin with François Truffaut” A short, dated-but-stable BFI feature that starts, honestly, with The 400 Blows.

subject: music
title: British Invasion (c. 1963–1967): the Atlantic flips
dek: UK bands sell America its own Black records back — while Motown, pirate radio, and Group Sounds run in the same years.
text: British Invasion (c. 1963–1967): the Atlantic flips UK bands sell America its own Black records back — while Motown, pirate radio, and Group Sounds run in the same years. c. 1963–1967 “British Invasion” is an American chart phrase from 1964. It names a sudden UK presence on Billboard, not a birth of rock and roll. The music had already been made — mostly in the United States, mostly by Black musicians. This capsule stays with 1963–1967. It does not cover punk. Music music 1950s The records US R&B and rock & roll reach Britain as imports, films, and the American Forces Network. 1962 Decca says no The Beatles audition in London on 1 January; Decca signs Brian Poole and the Tremeloes instead. 1964 Ed Sullivan 9 February: the Beatles live on CBS. About 73 million viewers. Billboard fills with UK names. 1964 Caroline Radio Caroline begins unlicensed broadcasts from a ship in the North Sea. 1966 Same years, elsewhere Motown and Stax still chart in the US. In Japan the Group Sounds boom is about to peak. 1967 The turn Sgt. Pepper, psychedelia, art-school volume. The Invasion name starts to look small. Seventy-three million on a Sunday Nielsen counted about 73 million viewers for the Beatles’ first live Ed Sullivan appearance on 9 February 1964 — a 45.3 rating and a 60 share, Sullivan’s first nightly win in seven years. They played five songs, including “I Want to Hold Your Hand.” The number is a television fact, not a measure of who invented the beat. British Invasion American trade-press name, from 1964, for the sudden run of UK acts on the Billboard charts after the Beatles’ first U.S. visit. It describes a market event, not the invention of the music. skiffle British 1950s craze: cheap instruments (guitar, washboard, tea-chest bass) playing American folk, blues, and Lonnie Donegan hits. A generation of UK musicians learned in skiffle groups before they bought electric guitars. R&B rhythm and blues U.S. Billboard’s postwar name for Black popular music. In Britain in the early 1960s, “R&B” also meant the harder, Chess-Records end of that catalogue — the records the Rolling Stones learned from. Ed Sullivan The Ed Sullivan Show Sunday-night CBS variety show. On 9 February 1964 the Beatles played live from Studio 50 in New York. Nielsen put the audience at about 73 million, a U.S. television record at the time. pirate radio Unlicensed stations on ships or offshore forts, 1964–67, that played pop the BBC would not. Radio Caroline began in March 1964. The Marine Broadcasting Offences Act 1967 shut most of them down. Beatlemania Press word, first common in Britain in late 1963, for the screaming, the airports, the haircuts. In the U.S. it arrives as a television event in February 1964. Decca British record company. On 1 January 1962 the Beatles recorded a 15-song audition at Decca Studios in West Hampstead. Decca passed and signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes, who had auditioned the same day. Group Sounds グループ・サウンズ ザ・タイガース Japanese 1960s electric-guitar pop, peaking about 1966–68. Bands such as ザ・タイガース (The Tigers) and テンプターズ (The Tempters) used the same imported records as Liverpool — inside a different industry of TV, agencies, and 歌謡曲. Motown Detroit label founded by Berry Gordy, 1959. In the mid-1960s it was not a prelude to the Invasion; it was a contemporary chart rival. The Supremes, the Temptations, and the Four Tops were on American radio the same weeks as the Beatles. Chess Records Chess Chicago label (Leonard and Phil Chess) that recorded Muddy Waters, Howlin’ Wolf, Chuck Berry, Bo Diddley. British R&B bands treated the catalogue as scripture and often failed to credit it as living music. Vox AC30 British amplifier company. The Vox AC30 is the small, bright stack in early Beatles and Stones photographs. It is one reason those records do not sound like Chicago club blues. Ready Steady Go! ITV pop show, 1963–66, that put British beat groups in front of a studio crowd. For UK viewers it mattered as much as Sullivan did for Americans. art school Several Invasion-era musicians (John Lennon, Keith Richards, Pete Townshend, Ray Davies) passed through British art colleges. The fact is used, sometimes too neatly, to explain why UK bands treated American R&B as material to redesign. Before Imported records, cheap guitars Rock and roll was already American, and already Black, before any British band had a U.S. work permit. Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Bo Diddley, and the Chess Records blues catalogue reached Britain as 78s and 45s, as films, and as signals from the American Forces Network. UK charts in the 1950s still treated Britain as a backwater that waited for the boat. Chuck Berry, about 1958. British beat groups learned his intros and his duck walk from records and from a few live dates. The photograph is a U.S. publicity still issued without a copyright notice; Beatles press photos from 1964 are not free to reuse. Chuck Berry in a light suit, holding an electric guitar, publicity photograph about 1958. The object, not the myth: Chess 1691, “Johnny B. Goode,” 1958. When a London band later played the riff on a Vox, they were selling this label’s music back to the country that had pressed it — often without saying so. Chess Records side-A label for Chuck Berry’s single Johnny B. Goode. In Britain the first cheap way in was skiffle: washboard, tea-chest bass, a guitar if you had one, Lonnie Donegan if you didn’t. John Lennon’s Quarrymen began as a skiffle group. So did half the beat groups that followed. Skiffle was not a style so much as a permission slip — you could start without a union card or a dance-band booking. By the early 1960s those kids had electric guitars and a weekly date in a cellar. Liverpool had the Cavern. London had the Crawdaddy and the Marquee. What they played was still, in large part, the American catalogue. The difference was volume, hair, and a class of art-school students who treated the catalogue as something you could redesign. The era The Atlantic flips — and does not empty On 1 January 1962 the Beatles recorded fifteen songs for Decca in West Hampstead. Decca passed and signed Brian Poole and the Tremeloes, who had auditioned the same day. The later line about “guitar groups” being finished is something Brian Epstein remembered and Dick Rowe denied. The rejection itself is not in dispute. EMI’s Parlophone, with George Martin, took them instead. In Britain, 1963 is already Beatlemania: “She Loves You,” the London Palladium, the Royal Variety Performance. In the United States the name still meant little until Capitol finally issued “I Want to Hold Your Hand” at the end of December 1963. On 9 February 1964 the band played live on The Ed Sullivan Show. About 73 million people watched. For American television that is the Invasion’s starting gun. For the music, it is a late scene. What followed on the Billboard Hot 100 was a list of British names: the Rolling Stones, the Kinks, the Who, the Animals, the Dave Clark Five, Dusty Springfield (who was not a beat group and is still part of the traffic). Many of the songs were American R&B rewritten at British volume. The Stones were blunter about the debt than the Beatles. Credit on the label and credit in the culture were not the same thing. A Vox AC30 Twin — the small, bright British amp in early Beatles and Stones photographs. Chicago blues through this box does not come out sounding like Chess studio tape. That difference is part of what the U.S. charts bought. A Vox AC30 Twin guitar amplifier, the compact British stack used by early-1960s beat groups. The BBC’s Light Programme still rationed pop. From March 1964, Radio Caroline and the other pirate radio ships played the records the BBC would not, from a ship in the North Sea. The audience was British teenagers. The legal theory was that the ship was outside the law. The Marine Broadcasting Offences Act of 1967 mostly ended the experiment. MV Caroline off the Isle of Man, summer 1965. Pirate radio is not a metaphor here. It is an unlicensed transmitter on a ship, playing 45s the BBC would not schedule. The radio ship MV Caroline at anchor off the Isle of Man in summer 1965. The same years, in the United States, the Invasion did not replace Black American music. Motown and Stax were not a prelude; they were on the radio the same weeks. The Supremes and the Beatles traded the number-one slot. A British band covering “Money” or “Twist and Shout” was taking a living catalogue, not a folk song from a dead singer. The same years, in Japan: Group Sounds. ザ・タイガース and テンプターズ used the same imported records — electric guitar, matching suits, television — inside a different industry of agencies and 歌謡曲. Hong Kong and Taiwan had their own mid-1960s beat groups, often hearing the records first on American Forces radio. None of this is a delayed copy of Sullivan. It is the same Atlantic (and Pacific) shipment of 45s, arriving in different booking systems. Orion TR8, made in Japan, 1960s. The Invasion is a story about records and television. It is also a story about cheap transistors — many of them Japanese — that let a teenager hear Caroline, Motown, or a Tokyo GS show without sitting in the family parlour. A Japanese-made Orion TR8 AM transistor radio from the 1960s. People Who is in the photograph, and who is on the label Chuck Berry 1926–2017 Guitar intros that British groups treated as a starter kit. “Johnny B. Goode” is 1958, Chess Records, St. Louis by way of Chicago. The Invasion makes less sense if he is only mentioned as an “influence.” Publicity photograph, about 1958. The Beatles active 1960–1970 Liverpool, skiffle, Hamburg residencies, then Parlophone. They are the Invasion’s television event. They are also a covers band that got very good at writing the next song. 1964 press photographs remain in copyright in the U.S.; this capsule does not pirate them. No free Beatles likeness here. The street is the period; the faces are still owned. Dusty Springfield 1939–1999 Not a beat-group boy. A British singer who took American soul seriously enough to go to Memphis later (Dusty in Memphis, 1969). In the Invasion years she is already on the UK charts, proof that the traffic was not only four boys and a Vox. ザ・タイガース / The Tigers debut 1967 Tokyo Group Sounds band (Sawada Kenji and others) on Japanese television in the same late-Invasion years. 「花の首飾り」 (1968) is a domestic hit, not an English cover. Same imported electric-guitar idea; different language, different industry. After Psychedelia, then a door By 1967 the Invasion name is already too small. Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, the Summer of Love as a press phrase, longer tracks, studio-as-instrument. The Who had already made volume and auto-destruction part of the act. The Kinks had already written English everyday life instead of American myth. What comes next is not this capsule. Psychedelia splits. Some of those musicians go pastoral, some go heavy, some go back to pubs. The later line toward pub rock and then punk is a door at the end of the corridor — visible, not walked through here. A question Leave this on the table If the hit is a British rewrite of a Chess Records 45, whose success are you counting? The Beatles — “I Want to Hold Your Hand” (live on The Ed Sullivan Show, 9 February 1964) Official TheBeatlesVEVO upload of the CBS performance. This is the clip, not a fan rip of the full hour. The Beatles’ own note on that Sullivan performance thebeatles.com page confirming the official VEVO release. Useful if the YouTube ID moves. Chuck Berry — “Johnny B. Goode” (1958 Chess single) Official UMG/Chess upload on the Chuck Berry Topic channel (“Provided to YouTube by Universal Music Group”). The 1958 single, not a live cover. ザ・タイガース / The Tigers — official catalogue (Universal Music Japan) Label page for the 1967–71 singles, including 「花の首飾り」. This is a rights-holder page, not a full-track pirate upload.

subject: feminism
title: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): who got to count as a “woman” in public
dek: Suffrage, splits, and the people the word “we” left out.
text: First Wave (c. 1848–1920): who got to count as a “woman” in public Suffrage, splits, and the people the word “we” left out. c. 1848–1920 “First wave” is a later Anglo-American label, not a name the people in this capsule used for themselves. It is useful as a frame — a span of public fights over whether women counted as political persons — and incomplete as a history. What follows uses the frame, then looks at the same decades elsewhere. Feminism feminism 1848 Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments; the vote among other grievances. 1851 Akron Sojourner Truth speaks. The famous refrain is a later rewrite. 1870 The split Fifteenth Amendment: race, not sex. Stanton and Anthony versus Stone and Douglass. 1907 Anqing Qiu Jin executed after the uprising. Same decade as British militancy, different state. 1913 Procession / Derby Washington, D.C. on 3 March; Emily Wilding Davison dies at Epsom. 1920 Nineteenth Amendment The vote, and Jim Crow still standing in the way. She copyrighted the shadow In 1864 Sojourner Truth registered the copyright on her own cartes-de-visite in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan — unusual for a sitter; the photographer usually claimed the image. The cards were printed “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” She sold them at lectures because lectures did not pay enough. The existing portrait in this capsule is one of those cards. coverture English common-law doctrine that a married woman’s legal identity was “covered” by her husband’s. Property, contracts, and wages were his unless a statute carved out an exception. separate spheres A nineteenth-century middle-class story: men in public/economic life, women in the home as a moral climate. It was a class rule as much as a sex rule. Wage-earning and enslaved women were never offered that delicacy. Seneca Falls Village in western New York. On 19–20 July 1848 a convention there issued the Declaration of Sentiments. “Seneca Falls” later became shorthand for the start of organized U.S. women’s rights — a useful date, not the only origin. Declaration of Sentiments Sentiments The 1848 Seneca Falls text, modeled on the Declaration of Independence. It listed grievances including the vote. The vote was not the only demand, and not everyone in the room wanted it named first. Fifteenth Amendment 15th Amendment Ratified 1870. It barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. The omission split the U.S. women’s-rights coalition. WSPU Women’s Social and Political Union Women’s Social and Political Union, founded 1903 by Emmeline Pankhurst. The militant wing of British suffrage: window-breaking, hunger strikes, and, in reply, force-feeding. Jim Crow The system of legal racial segregation and disenfranchisement in the U.S. South after Reconstruction — poll taxes, literacy tests, violence. The Nineteenth Amendment did not repeal it. 中國女報 Chinese Women’s Journal Chinese Women’s Journal, edited by Qiu Jin in Shanghai in 1907. Two issues appeared. It argued for women’s education and against bound feet in the same breath as anti-Qing politics. carte-de-visite cartes-de-visite A small albumen photograph mounted on card, cheap to reproduce, sold and collected in the 1860s. Sojourner Truth sold hers with a printed caption and a copyright in her own name. Gage Frances Dana Gage Frances Dana Gage. In 1863 she published a version of Sojourner Truth’s 1851 Akron speech that includes the refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. Nineteenth Amendment 19th Amendment Ratified 1920. It says the right to vote shall not be denied on account of sex. It did not touch poll taxes, literacy tests, or the violence that still blocked many Black women in the South. force-feeding In British prisons, hunger-striking suffragettes were restrained and fed through a tube. The Liberal government presented it as medical care. Militants presented it as assault. Both descriptions circulated in the press. doldrums A later weather report for U.S. organized feminism in the 1920s–1950s: the vote arrived, the coalition thinned. It describes one organized current going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended. Alice Paul American suffrage organizer, trained with British militants, then with Lucy Burns planned the 3 March 1913 Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington. Later the National Woman’s Party and the Equal Rights Amendment. Before Covered, separate, and already in training English common law treated a married woman as legally covered by her husband. The doctrine is called coverture. Her property, her contracts, her wages — the law did not see a separate person there. A single woman had more legal room; marriage closed it. Industrial work left the house. What remained, for middle-class white women, was a story about respectability: the home as a moral climate, the woman as domestic, delicate, and good. Historians call this “separate spheres.” It was a rule of class as much as of sex. Enslaved women, and women who worked for wages, were never offered that delicacy. They were already in public — as labor, as property, as exceptions the ideology did not have to explain. Abolition was the school many United States feminists came out of. They learned to petition, to lecture, to edit, to organize a room. The skills transferred. The alliance later cracked, when the question became which emancipation would be allowed to go first. The era A public “we,” and the people it could not hold In 1848, at Seneca Falls, New York, a convention issued a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence. The vote was among the grievances — not the only one, and not, at first, the one everyone in the room wanted named. The document still did something plain: it put women into the grammar of rights. A surviving copy of the Declaration of Sentiments signature page, including Eunice Foote. The 1848 text borrowed the Declaration of Independence’s cadence and then listed what that cadence had left out. Signature page of the 1848 Declaration of Sentiments, including Eunice Foote’s name. In 1851 Sojourner Truth spoke at a women’s rights meeting in Akron, Ohio. The famous refrain “Ain’t I a woman?” comes from Frances Dana Gage’s 1863 rewrite of that speech. Contemporary 1851 newspaper accounts do not use the refrain that way. The later version is the one that traveled. The historical point does not depend on the catchphrase. A feminism built on white middle-class delicacy treats enslaved women and working women as exceptions — bodies that have already been asked to do too much to count as the “woman” the movement is picturing. After the Civil War the coalition split over the Fifteenth Amendment (1870), which barred denying the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It did not mention sex. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony opposed ratifying without women. Lucy Stone and Frederick Douglass would not block Black men’s suffrage in order to wait. The argument was about sequence, and about who was being asked to stand aside. In Britain the movement divided by method: constitutional suffragists on one side, the militant Women’s Social and Political Union — Emmeline Pankhurst’s WSPU — on the other. Hunger strikes. Force-feeding. In 1913 Emily Wilding Davison died after stepping onto the course at the Epsom Derby. Emmeline Pankhurst in 1913, the year Davison died at Epsom and the WSPU’s militancy was impossible to ignore. Constitutional suffragists were still collecting signatures. Pankhurst’s organization was collecting prison time. Formal seated portrait of Emmeline Pankhurst, 1913. On 3 March 1913, the day before Wilson’s inauguration, Alice Paul and Lucy Burns organized the Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington, D.C. Inez Milholland rode in white on a white horse. Ida B. Wells was told that Black women should march in a rear contingent. She refused, and stepped into the Illinois delegation as it passed. The crowd on Pennsylvania Avenue, 3 March 1913. Men climbed poles and wagons to see. The procession was designed to be unmissable on the eve of an inauguration. Unmissable is not the same as welcomed: the parade was repeatedly broken by spectators stepping into the street. A dense crowd lining Pennsylvania Avenue to watch the 1913 woman suffrage procession in Washington, D.C. The official program for the same day. The horse, the banner, the Capitol: a picture of who the procession wanted to look like. Wells’s decision to leave the “rear contingent” is the part the program does not print. Color official program cover for the Woman Suffrage Procession, Washington, D.C., 3 March 1913, showing a woman on horseback before the Capitol. The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920. It did not undo Jim Crow. Many Black women in the South were still blocked by poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence. The amendment changed the federal text. The ground did not change with it. The same years, elsewhere: Qiu Jin 秋瑾 (1875–1907). She unbound her feet, studied in Japan, edited 中國女報 (the Chinese Women’s Journal), and was executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. Her public life does not sit on the Anglo-American staircase from Seneca Falls to 1920. It belongs in the same decades anyway — a woman deciding she would count in public, under a different state, and paying for it. People Four lives the frame has to stretch for Sojourner Truth c. 1797–1883 Born enslaved in New York. She sold cartes-de-visite captioned “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” The card was a living. It was also an argument about who owned the image of a woman who had been treated as property. Carte-de-visite, 1864. “I sell the shadow to support the substance.” Ida B. Wells 1862–1931 Anti-lynching journalist; Southern Horrors appeared in 1892. She treated suffrage and racial terror as one fight, which is why a segregated parade order was not a small slight. She walked into the Illinois line instead. Ida B. Wells-Barnett, photograph by Mary Garrity, c. 1893. Inez Milholland 1886–1916 Lawyer and the image the 1913 procession needed at its head. She died in 1916 on a western suffrage tour, at thirty. The photograph outlived the campaign she was riding for. The 1913 visual: white cape, white horse, Pennsylvania Avenue. Qiu Jin 秋瑾 1875–1907 Unbound feet. Study in Japan. Editor of 中國女報. Executed after the 1907 Anqing uprising. If “first wave” cannot hold her, the phrase is too small — not her life. Qiu Jin, photographed between 1900 and 1907. A story The shadow and the substance Sojourner Truth, 1864. She sold the card because lectures did not pay enough. She also put her own copyright on it. Sojourner Truth’s 1864 carte-de-visite, with the printed line I sell the shadow to support the substance under her portrait. Truth sold her image because lectures did not pay enough. The “shadow” is the photograph — a thing that can be reproduced, captioned, passed from hand to hand. The “substance” is the work, and the body that had been treated as property. She put the sentence on the card in English, under her own name, and made the sale part of the argument: I will be paid for the copy of me that you can hold. Keep the card in mind when a movement talks about “women” as if the category were already settled. Someone is always deciding which body is the subject, and which body is the illustration. After The vote, the doldrums, and the staircase In the United States the 1920s through the 1950s are often called the “doldrums”: the vote arrived, the coalition thinned. The word is a weather report written after the fact. It describes a particular organized feminism going quiet. It does not mean the questions ended. What gets called the second wave — the 1960s and 1970s — turned to the workplace, to sexuality, to housework. “The personal is political.” The who-counts problem returned in public, including in the Combahee River Collective statement of 1977, which refused to treat race, sex, and class as separate queues. The wave metaphor itself is the after. It offers a tidy staircase: first the vote, then the rest. It hides the people who were never on the stairs — and the fights that did not wait for the next numbered swell. A question Leave this on the table When a movement says “we,” who is being asked to wait? Time to Remember — Time of the Suffragettes (1911–1913) British Pathé compilation of British suffragette newsreel, 1911–1913. This is not film of the 1913 Washington procession. The Derby — 1912 & 1913 British Pathé racing newsreel. It includes the 1913 Epsom Derby, when Emily Wilding Davison stepped onto the course. Again: Britain, not Pennsylvania Avenue.
